Auto-tune

The bot tweaks its own numbers over time. While it is running, a few clones of it trade the exact same tokens on paper, each with its settings nudged a little (a bit higher take profit here, a tighter stop loss there). After every round of launches the clones are compared with the real bot, launch by launch. If some of them clearly did better than luck would explain, the bot moves part of the way toward them. Then a new round starts around the new numbers.

What it cannot do. It cannot create an edge that is not there: if no setting works, it mostly stays put (and now and then follows a lucky streak). On simulated (made-up) data it only learns the made-up market. When a recording plays again from the start it pauses, because tuning on data the bot has already seen would only be memorising. Paper only: nothing here touches a wallet.
Start the bot — clones only run while it trades.
This is the demo market. Auto-tune can only learn this made-up market, so its changes say nothing about real trading.

How it tunes

How many copies of the bot run side by side (2 to 8). More clones try more ideas, but the bar for proof goes up.
How many new tokens to watch before judging the clones (20 to 1000). Longer rounds are slower but harder to fool.
How sure it must be that a clone really beat the bot, and was not just lucky. Higher means fewer changes.
How far the bot moves toward the winning clones; 0.5 = halfway. (0.1 to 1)

Changing anything here, or in the bot's settings, starts a fresh round.

What this is

A paper-trading simulator. It models the pump.fun fee, a per-transaction cost and a delay between decision and fill, but not other bots racing you or dropped transactions. Real results would be worse than what you see here.
